title: Academic Writing and Referencing
summary: How to answer an essay question, build clear paragraphs and sentences, use sources honestly and reference them correctly.

lessons.title: Reading the question and forming an argument

body.p: Most essays lose marks before the first sentence is written, because the writer answered a different question from the one set. Start by breaking the question into its parts: the command word, the topic, and any limits such as a time period, country or theory.

list: Discuss: examine different views and reach a reasoned position.
Evaluate or assess: judge how strong, effective or valid something is, using evidence.
Compare: show similarities and differences, and say what they mean.
Analyse: break something into parts and explain how they relate.
Critically examine: question the evidence and assumptions, not only describe them.

body.p: Question: 'Evaluate the effectiveness of mobile money in improving financial inclusion in East Africa.' Command word: evaluate. Topic: mobile money and financial inclusion. Limit: East Africa. A weak answer describes how mobile money works. A strong answer decides how effective it has been, using criteria such as access, cost and use by low-income users, and supports each point with evidence.

A thesis is your answer to the question in one or two sentences. It should take a position that can be argued. Weak: 'This essay will look at mobile money.' Better: 'Mobile money has widened access to basic payments, but high transaction costs and limited credit products mean its effect on deeper financial inclusion has been smaller.' Every paragraph should then help to support this position.

steps: Underline the command word and topic.
Brainstorm what you already know and what you need to find.
Write a draft thesis in one or two sentences.
List three or four main points that support it.
Check the marking criteria or assignment brief, and ask your tutor if anything is unclear.

body.tip: Your thesis may change as you read. Rewrite it before you write the final draft so that the introduction matches the conclusion.

lessons.title: Building paragraphs that do one job

body.p: A paragraph develops one main idea. If you can say the paragraph's point in one sentence, it is probably well focused. If it contains two unrelated points, split it. If a sentence does not support the point, remove it or move it.

list: Point: a topic sentence stating the paragraph's main claim.
Evidence: a fact, statistic, example or source that supports the claim.
Explanation: why the evidence supports the claim and how it answers the question.
Link: connect back to the essay question or forward to the next paragraph.

body.p: The most common weakness is missing explanation. Students place evidence and assume the reader sees its meaning. The examiner is marking your reasoning, so spell it out.
Before: 'Many students in Lagos use public transport. Fares have risen. This is a problem. Some students walk.' After:

body.code: Rising transport costs are limiting some students' attendance at lectures. For example, if a student's daily fare increases from N400 to N700, the weekly cost over five days rises by N1,500, which is a substantial share of a limited allowance. As a result, some students choose to walk long distances or miss early classes. This suggests that transport policy is an educational issue as well as a transport one.

body.p: The after version has a point (costs limit attendance), evidence (the fare calculation), explanation (what students do as a result) and a link (why it matters). The numbers are an illustration, not real data; in your own essay you would cite a source for any real figures.

An introduction gives brief context, defines key terms, states your thesis and outlines the structure. A conclusion restates your answer, summarises the main reasoning and notes limits. Do not introduce new evidence in the conclusion.

body.tip: Read only the first sentence of each paragraph. Together they should outline your argument.

body.p: Academic style is not about long words. It is about precision, clear logic and a neutral tone. Your reader should understand each sentence on first reading.

list: Prefer the active voice when the actor matters: 'The researchers surveyed 200 farmers' is clearer than 'A survey was carried out'.
Use specific verbs and nouns instead of vague words such as 'thing', 'stuff' or 'a lot'.
Avoid contractions, slang and spoken fillers in formal work.
Qualify claims honestly: 'suggests' and 'is associated with' are more accurate than 'proves' when the evidence is limited.
Keep one main idea in each sentence and break up very long sentences.

body.p: Before: 'It is a well-known fact that a lot of students nowadays don't really manage their time well and this causes them to get bad marks in exams.' This sentence is wordy, makes an unsupported claim and uses vague wording.

After: 'Several studies report that poor time management is associated with lower exam performance (Author, Year).' It is shorter, hedged appropriately and points to a source. Here 'Author, Year' stands for a real citation you would supply.

Another example. Before: 'The experiment was done by the group and the results were looked at and it was found that the yield was higher.' After: 'The group measured the yield and found that it was higher under the treated conditions.' The after sentence names the actor, uses precise verbs and gives the condition.

Use connectives to show logic: 'however' for contrast, 'therefore' for result, 'for example' for illustration, 'in addition' for extension. Do not use them as decoration. A connective is a promise about the relationship between two ideas, so check the relationship is really there.

body.tip: Read your draft aloud. Where you run out of breath or stumble, the sentence is probably too long or unclear.

lessons.title: Using sources honestly: quoting, paraphrasing, summarising

body.p: Academic work joins an existing conversation. You show what others have found, then add your own analysis. Sources give your claims authority, but only when you credit them. Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, whether you copied directly, changed a few words, or reused your own earlier assessed work without permission. Institutions treat it seriously, and rules and penalties vary, so check your institution's guidelines and ask your tutor if you are unsure.

body.h: Three ways to use a source

list: Direct quotation: exact words in quotation marks with a page number. Use sparingly, for striking or technical wording.
Paraphrase: restating a specific idea in your own words and sentence structure. It still needs a citation.
Summary: a short overview of a longer text or the main point of a section, also cited.

body.p: Original text (invented for this example): 'Spaced practice, in which study sessions are separated by intervals of time, tends to produce better long-term retention than massed practice.'

Poor paraphrase, still too close: 'Spaced practice, where sessions are separated by time, tends to produce better long-term retention than massed practice (Okafor, 2020).' Only a few words changed. A good paraphrase: 'Spreading study over several days helps students remember material longer than cramming it into one sitting (Okafor, 2020).'

steps: Check who wrote it and whether they have relevant expertise.
Prefer peer-reviewed articles, academic books and official reports for evidence.
Check the date, since some fields change quickly.
Look for evidence behind the claims, not only opinion.
Compare at least two sources before relying on a surprising claim.

body.tip: Take notes with the source details beside every idea, so you never have to guess later where a point came from.

lessons.title: Referencing: in-text citations and reference lists

body.p: Referencing has two parts. An in-text citation, placed where you use the idea, points to the source briefly. A reference list at the end gives the full details so the reader can find it. Every in-text citation must match an entry in the list, and the reverse. Styles vary by department and institution, and even Harvard has local versions, so always follow your institution's guidelines. The patterns below are common versions.

body.code:
In text: (Okafor, 2020) or Okafor (2020); with a quotation: (Okafor, 2020, p. 14)
Book: Okafor, N. (2020). Writing for university study (2nd ed.). Example Press.
Web page: Mensah, K. (2023, March 5). How to plan a literature search. Example University Library. https://www.example.edu/literature-search

In text: (Okafor, 2020) or Okafor (2020); with a quotation: (Okafor, 2020, p. 14)
Book: Okafor, N. (2020) Writing for university study. 2nd edn. London: Example Press.
Web page: Mensah, K. (2023) How to plan a literature search. Available at: https://www.example.edu/literature-search (Accessed: 12 May 2024).

body.p: All authors and publishers above are invented for illustration. Notice the differences: APA places the year in brackets after the author and puts the date and site name in a particular order; many Harvard versions add an accessed date for web pages and the place of publication for books. Details such as italics for titles, capital letters and punctuation also differ between styles.

list: Record full details when you find a source: author, year, title, publisher or website, URL, and access date.
Cite as you write, not at the end.
Arrange the reference list alphabetically by the author's surname.
Use a reference manager if your institution recommends one, but still check the output.
If there is no author, follow your style guide on using the organisation or the title.

body.tip: When a web page has no date, your style guide will say how to show that. Do not invent a date.

body.p: Strong writers separate writing from editing. A first draft gets your ideas on the page. Editing, done later, improves structure, clarity and accuracy. Mixing both at once is slow and tends to produce neither good ideas nor clean sentences.

Suppose an essay of 2,000 words is due in two weeks. Spend the first few days reading and note-taking, then make an outline. Write the first draft over the next few days, aiming for something like 400 to 500 words per sitting. Leave at least two days away from the text before you edit, since you will notice problems more easily. Keep a day at the end for formatting and references.

steps: Argument: does every paragraph support the thesis and answer the question?
Structure: are the paragraphs in a logical order, with clear topic sentences?
Evidence: is each claim backed up and every source cited?
Sentences: remove repetition, tighten long sentences and replace vague words.
Proofreading: check spelling, grammar, punctuation, numbering, headings and the reference list.

list: Paragraphs with evidence but no explanation.
Using 'they' or 'this' without a clear referent.
Inconsistent tense when discussing sources, for example mixing 'argues' and 'argued' without reason.
A reference list that does not match the in-text citations.
Exceeding or falling far below the word limit. Check your institution's rules on how word counts work.

body.p: Spell-checkers miss correct words used wrongly, such as 'affect' and 'effect' or 'their' and 'there'. Read the text slowly, use a different font or print it, and ask a friend to read it. If your institution allows writing support services, a visit to the writing centre can help. Also check your institution's policy on using AI tools, since it varies.

body.tip: Keep a personal checklist of your own repeated mistakes and check for those first.

quiz.q: An essay question asks you to 'Evaluate the impact of remittances on household welfare in Ghana.' Which opening plan best fits the command word?
options: Judge how large and how reliable the impact is, using evidence for each criterion
Compare remittances with every other source of household income in all African countries and regions
Describe what remittances are and list famous examples
Give the history of money transfer from the 1800s

quiz.q: Which is the strongest thesis statement?
options: Social media is something that a large number of university students use every day for many purposes.
This essay will discuss social media and study.
Social media is bad.
Heavy social media use can reduce study quality, but structured limits mean students can benefit from its collaborative features.

quiz.q: A paragraph states a claim and gives a statistic, then moves on. According to PEEL, what is most likely missing?
options: A second statistic
Explanation of how the evidence supports the claim
A direct quotation
A longer introduction

quiz.q: You read only the first sentence of each paragraph in your draft and they do not outline an argument. What does this suggest?
options: The sentences are all too short and need to be joined into longer ones across the whole essay
The essay needs more quotations
The conclusion is too long
The topic sentences or paragraph order need work

quiz.q: Which rewrite of 'A lot of people think the results were bad' is most suitable for academic work?
options: Many people feel that the results were really quite bad overall, and this was clear to most of them.
Some commentators described the results as unsatisfactory (Author, Year).
The results were bad, as everyone knows.
Results bad.

quiz.q: The evidence on a topic is limited and from one small study. Which wording is the most accurate?
options: The study proves that the method works.
The method always works.
The study suggests that the method may help, though more evidence is needed.
Nobody can say anything about the method.

quiz.q: A student changes three words in a sentence from an article and includes no citation. How should this be judged?
options: Acceptable, because the words are changed
Likely plagiarism, because the idea and structure belong to the source and are not credited
Acceptable if the article is old
Acceptable if it is only one sentence

quiz.q: When is a direct quotation most appropriate?
options: When the exact wording is distinctive or technical and you reference the page
In place of explaining the idea yourself, because quotations show that you have read widely and carefully
To fill space when you are short of words
Whenever a source is by a famous author

quiz.q: Which source is usually the strongest evidence for a claim about research findings?
options: A peer-reviewed article reporting the study
An anonymous forum post that repeats the claim confidently and has received many comments and likes
A social media video
A friend's summary

quiz.q: What is the difference between an in-text citation and a reference list?
options: They are the same thing in different places, and you only need one of them in an essay
The citation gives full details and the list gives only the surname
The citation points briefly to a source where it is used, and the list gives full details to find it
The reference list is optional if you quote

quiz.q: Which feature is typical of many Harvard web page references but not of the APA pattern shown in the course?
options: Listing the author's name or names at the start of the reference, followed by the year
Giving the year
An 'Available at' phrase and an accessed date
Using a URL

quiz.q: You finish a 2,000-word essay the night before it is due. What is the best editing approach available?
options: Edit the sentences first and skip the argument check, because the sentences are what the reader sees first
Proofread only spelling
Read only the introduction
Check argument and structure first, then evidence, then sentences, then proofread, as time allows
